discovery: Theory of defect-mediated two-dimensional melting and prediction of the hexatic phase
subfield: Condensed matter physics (statistical mechanics, soft matter)
motivation: Building on Kosterlitz and Thouless, Halperin and Nelson, and independently Young, showed that two-dimensional crystals melt in two stages through the unbinding of dislocations and then disclinations. Between the solid and the liquid lies a new state of matter: the hexatic, with quasi-long-range bond-orientational order but short-range translational order. This was a real prediction of a new broken symmetry, derived from the topology of defects. It has since been confirmed in colloidal monolayers, freely suspended liquid-crystal films, electrons on helium and hard-disk simulations. The KTHNY framework turned defect topology into a quantitative tool, and bond-orientational order now runs through the physics of liquid crystals, colloids, active matter, glasses and biological membranes. The 2016 prize recognized topological transitions. This completes that story with the discovery of an entirely new phase that the topology demands.
